title: Al-Batin, the Hidden
tomorrow: what do your hands do when you finally stop managing everything?

cards: Your glasses are on your head while you search the whole house for them. The thing you can't find is sometimes the thing that's too close. The last Name of the verse is Al-Batin, the Inward, the Hidden.
And Muslim thinkers have given yesterday's question two honest answers. Is He hidden because He's far beyond us, or because He's nearer than we can see?

teach.b: The first view leans on a verse that, in Pickthall's words, says: "Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision."
On this reading, Al-Batin means beyond. No eye, no mind, no feeling can wrap itself around who God is. We know Him through His Names and His signs, never by seeing past them.
Its best point is a humble one: whatever you picture, God is not that, so no one gets to claim they've caught Him in a picture.
The second view, found among Sufi writers, leans on another verse: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." On this reading, He's hidden the way light is hidden.
You don't look at the light in a room; you look at everything it shows you.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: TOO NEAR TO SEE.
teach.b: Hidden by being everywhere, too near to stand back from.
Its best point is a warm one: on your loneliest night, the Hidden isn't far off.

Both views can pray the same du'a from Sahih Muslim, the one the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught for bedtime: You are the Inward, and there is nothing beyond You. One camp hears beyond as above every grasp.
The other hears it as closer than anything. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the same Name can make a person feel very small, and very held.

how: Muslims recite the four Names of 57:3 in the Prophet's bedtime du'a; theologians and Sufi writers have discussed what it means that Allah is al-Batin.

o: the Hidden, beyond what the senses grasp
the Absent, who stays far above the world
the Secret, who keeps His plans from us

games.q: who says what about the Hidden — tap the pairs.
p: view two: too near to see

s: Al-Batin means God is absent or far off
one view says hidden because beyond every grasp; the other, hidden because so near. neither says absent.
a verse says vision cannot grasp Him
"Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision."
Muslim thinkers have read al-Batin only one way
some stress that He's beyond any grasp; Sufi writers often, that He's hidden by nearness.

games.q: your friend asks, 'if God's real, why can't i feel Him?' you give the 'too near to see' answer. what would the other camp add, at its best?
o: He's beyond every sense, so not feeling Him proves nothing; you know Him by His signs.
feeling God is the whole point, so if you don't, something in you is broken.
that's a question you shouldn't ask; faith means never wondering.
games.why: view one's best case: vision comprehendeth Him not. not feeling Him isn't evidence against Him; His Names and signs are how He's known.

practice: Listen for the quietest sound in the room: the hum of a fridge, the air, your own breathing. Stay with that one sound for the sit. It was there all along, too close to notice, until you listened.

wordCard.voice: Al-Batin. The Hidden, the Inward: beyond what the senses grasp, and, some say, nearer than the vein in your neck.

orig.note: Arabic: the Hidden, the Inward. the fourth Name of 57:3.

carryVoice: The line to keep: hidden, whether far beyond or very near, and the riddle is whole now. Peace till tomorrow.

sources.q: Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision.
We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2713 (bedtime du'a: You are the Inward, there is nothing beyond You)
